narration: You type google dot com and press enter. Before you can even blink, four computers have teamed up just to find where Google lives.
Because computers don't route by names. They route by numbers, called IP addresses.
So your laptop first asks a DNS resolver, usually run by your internet provider.
The resolver doesn't know the answer yet, so it starts at the very top, with a root server.
The root doesn't know Google, but it knows who runs dot com, and sends the resolver there.
The dot com server points it one step further, to the servers Google runs itself.
And Google's own server finally replies with the real answer, the IP address.
The resolver passes it back to your laptop, and only now can the actual connection to Google begin.
Here's the clever part. The resolver keeps that answer in its cache for a set time, called the time to live.
So when the next person asks, the answer comes back instantly, with no trip to the root at all.
That's DNS. The internet's phone book, looked up billions of times every single day.
